subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Geography simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which three resources are the main focus of the 'challenge of resource management'?
questions.explain: Food, water and energy are the three essential resources needed for economic and social well-being that this topic examines.

questions.q: Why is the global distribution of resources described as UNEVEN?
options: Every country has exactly the same resources
Some regions are rich in resources such as fertile land or fossil fuels while others have very few, due to physical and economic factors
Resources are shared equally by international law
questions.explain: Physical geography (climate, geology) and economic development mean some areas have plentiful resources and others are resource-poor, creating global inequality in access.

questions.q: Which factor most affects a country's access to WATER resources?
options: Climate and the availability of rivers, lakes and groundwater
The number of TV channels available
The colour of the national flag
questions.explain: Physical factors such as climate (rainfall) and the presence of surface and groundwater, plus wealth to build infrastructure, largely determine water availability.

questions.q: Global demand for food, water and energy is RISING mainly because of...
options: A growing world population and rising wealth/consumption in emerging economies
Falling population and lower living standards
questions.explain: Population growth, economic development, industrialisation and rising affluence all increase demand for food, water and energy across the world.

questions.q: A rapidly developing (emerging) country typically sees its energy demand...
options: Rise as industry, transport and household use grow
questions.explain: Industrialisation, more vehicles and higher living standards raise energy demand quickly in emerging economies such as India and China.

questions.q: 'Resource security' means...
options: Having a reliable, affordable and sustainable supply of a resource to meet a population's needs
Using up resources as fast as possible
questions.explain: Resource security exists when a country can reliably access enough affordable food, water or energy for its people, now and in the future.

questions.q: Which situation best shows resource INSECURITY?
options: A country facing frequent droughts and unable to supply enough safe water to its population
A country generating more electricity than it needs
A country with plentiful, reliable clean water for all
questions.explain: Resource insecurity occurs when supply cannot meet demand, e.g. water scarcity from drought, leading to shortages, conflict or reliance on imports.

questions.q: A common CONSEQUENCE of resource insecurity is...
options: An immediate end to all trade
Rising prices, potential conflict and greater reliance on imports
questions.explain: When resources are scarce, prices rise, competition and even conflict can occur, and countries may become dependent on imports or exploit fragile environments.

questions.q: Roughly how much water does the average person in the UK use per day?
questions.explain: The average UK person uses around 150 litres of water a day for domestic uses such as washing, flushing and cooking.

questions.q: There is a water SUPPLY imbalance in the UK because...
options: Water demand is highest where rainfall is greatest
The whole country has identical rainfall
The wetter north and west have most rainfall, but the drier, more populated south and east have highest demand
questions.explain: Highest rainfall is in the north and west, but greatest population and demand are in the south-east, creating a mismatch addressed by water transfer schemes.

questions.q: How has the UK's ENERGY mix changed in recent years?
options: Renewables (especially wind and solar) have grown while coal use has fallen sharply
It has stopped importing all energy
It relies more heavily on coal than ever before
questions.explain: The UK has cut coal dramatically and expanded renewables; on many days around a third of UK electricity now comes from renewable sources such as wind.

questions.q: A water TRANSFER scheme increases supply by...
options: Moving water from areas of surplus to areas of deficit, e.g. via pipelines or canals
questions.explain: Water transfer moves water from wetter surplus regions to drier deficit regions where demand is high, though it can be costly and disrupt ecosystems.

questions.q: Which is a SUSTAINABLE way to manage water supply?
options: Wasting water to keep prices low
Improving efficiency, fixing leaks and using metering to reduce demand
questions.explain: Sustainable water management focuses on conservation: reducing leaks, water metering, efficient appliances and greywater recycling to balance supply and demand.

questions.q: Building a DAM and reservoir helps water supply, but a drawback is that it...
options: Provides no water storage at all
Can flood land, displace people and disrupt river ecosystems
Reduces the amount of stored water
questions.explain: Dams store water and can generate HEP, but flooding valleys displaces communities, drowns habitats and alters sediment flow downstream.

questions.q: Which strategy increases energy supply using a RENEWABLE source?
options: Opening a new coal-fired power station
questions.explain: Offshore wind is renewable. Coal, oil and gas (including fracked shale gas) are non-renewable fossil fuels that emit carbon and will run out.

questions.q: Improving energy EFFICIENCY (e.g. insulation and LED lighting) helps because it...
options: Reduces demand so existing supplies last longer and emissions fall
Increases the amount of energy wasted
Forces greater reliance on fossil fuels
questions.explain: Using energy more efficiently cuts demand, meaning less needs to be generated, which saves money, conserves resources and lowers carbon emissions.

questions.q: Which is an example of SUSTAINABLE food production?
options: Organic farming, permaculture and locally sourced ('agri-tech'/low-input) food to reduce environmental harm
Clearing rainforest for large monoculture plantations
questions.explain: Sustainable food production (e.g. organic farming, permaculture, seasonal/local sourcing) meets food needs while protecting soils, water and biodiversity for the future.

questions.q: Reducing FOOD MILES (the distance food travels) is sustainable because it...
options: Lowers transport emissions and can support local producers
questions.explain: Sourcing food locally and seasonally cuts the emissions from transporting it long distances and can strengthen local economies.

questions.q: Which is an ENVIRONMENTAL impact of extracting fossil fuels (e.g. fracking or mining)?
options: A guaranteed fall in global temperatures
Water and air pollution, land disturbance and possible groundwater contamination
questions.explain: Extracting fossil fuels can pollute water and air, disturb land and habitats, and fracking raises concerns about groundwater contamination and minor earth tremors.

questions.q: A major global impact of burning fossil fuels for energy is...
options: An increase in the ozone layer
Increased carbon dioxide emissions contributing to climate change
questions.explain: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, enhancing the greenhouse effect and driving global climate change.
